content: Vaginitis refers to inflammation or infection of the vagina. It can present with various symptoms, causes, and treatment options, which are detailed below: Symptoms of Vaginitis: 1. Irritation and itching in the genital area. 2. Inflammation of the labia majora, labia minora, or perineal area, which may include redness, swelling, and irritation. 3. Vaginal discharge, which may vary in consistency and color depending on the underlying cause. 4. Foul vaginal odor, which can be particularly noticeable in certain infections. 5. Discomfort or burning sensation during urination, which may indicate irritation or infection. Causes of Vaginitis: Vaginitis can affect women of all ages and is a common condition. It may be caused by: Bacteria, yeasts, viruses, or other parasites. Sexually transmitted infections (STIs), such as trichomoniasis or gonorrhea. Chemical irritants, including bubble baths, soaps, perfumes, vaginal contraceptives, and feminine sprays. Environmental factors, such as poor hygiene or allergens. Candida albicans, a yeast that commonly causes yeast infections, leading to genital itching and thick, white vaginal discharge. Antibiotic use, which can disrupt the normal vaginal flora and promote yeast overgrowth. Bacterial vaginosis, an overgrowth of certain bacteria in the vagina, often causing a thin, gray discharge with a fishy odor. Trichomonas vaginalis, a sexually transmitted parasite, which can cause genital itching, a strong vaginal odor, and heavy yellow-gray or green discharge. Tight or non-absorbent clothing, which can create a warm, damp environment conducive to infections. Postmenopausal estrogen deficiency, which can lead to vaginal dryness, thinning of the vaginal and vulvar skin, and increased susceptibility to irritation and infection. Skin conditions that cause chronic vulvar itching and irritation. Foreign bodies, such as forgotten tampons, which can lead to irritation, itching, and foul-smelling discharge. Non-specific vulvovaginitis, which is more common in prepubertal girls and may be associated with poor genital hygiene or bacterial overgrowth from stool contamination. Risk Factors: Vaginitis is common across all age groups. Risk factors include exposure to irritants, poor hygiene, hormonal changes, and sexual activity. In children, unusual infections or recurrent episodes of unexplained vulvovaginitis may raise concerns about sexual abuse. When to Seek Medical Care: Contact a healthcare provider if symptoms of vaginitis are present or if known vaginitis does not respond to treatment. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider will perform a pelvic examination to assess for redness, tenderness, or other abnormalities in the vulva or vagina. A wet prep (microscopic evaluation of vaginal discharge) is often performed to identify yeast, bacteria, or other organisms. In some cases, a culture of the vaginal discharge may be done to identify the specific organism causing the infection. A biopsy of irritated vulvar tissue may be recommended if no infection is detected. Treatment Options: Treatment depends on the underlying cause and may include: Antibiotics, either oral or topical, for bacterial infections. Antifungal creams for yeast infections. Antibacterial creams for certain bacterial overgrowths. Cortisone creams to reduce inflammation. Antihistamines for allergic reactions causing irritation. Estrogen creams for postmenopausal women with low estrogen levels contributing to symptoms. Proper genital hygiene is essential, especially for infections caused by bacteria from stool contamination. Sitz baths may be recommended to soothe irritation. Allowing more air to reach the genital area can be helpful. This can be achieved by: Wearing cotton underwear or underwear with a cotton lining in the crotch area to improve airflow and reduce moisture. Removing underwear at bedtime. Special Considerations for STIs: If a sexually transmitted infection is diagnosed, it is crucial that all sexual partners receive treatment, even if they are asymptomatic. Failure to treat partners can result in reinfection. Prognosis: With proper treatment, infections causing vaginitis are usually effectively resolved.
